title: Politics and weak oversight fuel health sector graft, BHW says
excerpt: Bangladesh Health Watch's 2025-26 report documents losses in drug procurement, doctor absenteeism and commissions paid for diagnostic referrals.
content:
Political influence and weak oversight are driving corruption in Bangladesh's health sector, according to a report by Bangladesh Health Watch (BHW), a civil society network, launched in Dhaka on 15 November, The Daily Star reported.

The biennial report for 2025-26, titled Challenging Corruption: Strengthening Governance in Bangladesh's Health Sector, has 11 chapters written by 17 researchers. Shams El Arifeen, senior scientist at icddr,b, presented the findings at the International Mother Language Institute.

Key findings

  • Diagnostic centres paid referring doctors 20 to 50 percent of test charges. The report estimates such commissions could reach Tk 1,861 crore a year, a figure it says needs independent checking.
  • Citing media investigations, the report says procurement at the Central Medical Stores Depot (CMSD) caused losses of Tk 459 crore, with some supplies bought at up to 18 times their fair value. Equipment worth Tk 283 crore was lying unused.
  • The Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council received 172 complaints between 2010 and May 2025. 79 are pending and 29 led to disciplinary action.
  • About 40 percent of doctors were absent during unannounced visits.
  • The number of medical colleges grew from 62 in 2010 to 118 in 2022-23.

BHW convener Ahmed Mushtaque Raza Chowdhury, State Minister for Health MA Muhit and Swedish Ambassador Nicolas Weeks were among those at the launch, which was chaired by BHW Advisory Group member Halida Hanum Akhter.

Why it matters

Money lost in procurement and commissions is money not spent on patients, and absent doctors push poor families towards private care. For NGOs working on health rights and social accountability, the report offers documented evidence to use in monitoring and advocacy, at a time when the government is promising to fill vacant posts.

What to watch

Whether the health ministry acts on the procurement and absenteeism findings, and whether the medical council speeds up its handling of complaints.
